title: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide (Volume 1)
author: Alex Xu
why: Read the opening chapters for the four-step interview framework and back-of-the-envelope estimation, then the rate limiter, consistent hashing and unique ID generator chapters as compact worked answers to the most-asked building-block questions.

title: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide (Volume 2)
author: Alex Xu and Sahn Lam
why: Harder, more domain-specific cases than Volume 1: use the distributed message queue, S3-like object storage, ad click aggregation and payment system chapters to practise designs where storage layout and exactly-once effects decide the answer.

title: Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems
author: Betsy Beyer, Chris Jones, Jennifer Petoff and Niall Richard Murphy (eds.), Google
why: The full book, free online: read chapters 3 to 6 for error budgets, SLOs and symptom-based monitoring, and chapters 21 and 22 for load shedding and how cascading failures start.

title: The Site Reliability Workbook: Practical Ways to Implement SRE
author: Betsy Beyer, Niall Richard Murphy, David K. Rensin, Kent Kawahara and Stephen Thorne (eds.), Google
why: The hands-on companion to the SRE book: it turns SLOs into concrete burn-rate alert rules and error budget policies, and has chapters on canarying releases and managing load.

title: High Performance Browser Networking
author: Ilya Grigorik (O'Reilly)
why: Read the TCP and TLS chapters to see where handshake round trips and slow start go on a real page load, and the HTTP/2 and WebSocket chapters for why multiplexing and long-lived connections change server design.

title: Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data
author: Fay Chang et al. (OSDI 2006)
why: The origin of the wide-column model: read it for the row/column-family/timestamp data model, memtables flushed to immutable SSTables with compactions, and tablets as the unit of sharding, which HBase and Cassandra's storage engine both inherit.

title: Netflix Technology Blog
author: Netflix engineering
why: Search it for the posts behind Chaos Monkey, Hystrix-style circuit breaking and adaptive concurrency limits: the reasoning for designing a large microservice fleet to keep serving while its parts fail.

title: Uber Engineering Blog
author: Uber engineering
why: Read it for what happens after microservices go too far: posts on its domain-oriented microservice architecture, schemaless storage on top of MySQL, and geospatial indexing at city scale.

title: Discord Engineering Blog
author: Discord engineering
why: Follow its message-storage posts (MongoDB to Cassandra to ScyllaDB) for hot partitions in a wide-column store, and its Elixir posts for holding millions of concurrent WebSocket connections.

title: Stripe Engineering Blog
author: Stripe engineering
why: Short, concrete posts from a payments API that cannot double-charge: idempotent retries, the rate limiters and load shedders in front of its API, canonical log lines, and online data migrations.

title: The Cloudflare Blog
author: Cloudflare
why: The best public source of detailed outage post-mortems and DDoS write-ups, plus posts on anycast routing and running code at the edge; read a post-mortem end to end to see how one config push becomes a global incident.

title: Engineering at Meta
author: Meta engineering
why: Read the TAO and cache-consistency posts for how a read-heavy social graph is served from caches, and why invalidation races, not hit ratio, are the hard part at that scale.

title: Shopify Engineering
author: Shopify engineering
why: The clearest public case for a modular monolith over microservices, plus posts on splitting a large Rails/MySQL deployment into isolated pods by shop and surviving flash-sale traffic spikes.
